title: Bit tricks at interview
objectives: Use XOR, masks and shifts for the classic bit problems.

screens.title: The odd one out
screens.prose: Every number in `[4, 1, 2, 1, 2]` appears twice except one. Below, each is written in binary. Try pairing them off by hand.
screens.question: Combine all five with XOR, `^`, which sets a bit where exactly one side has it. What is `4 ^ 1 ^ 2 ^ 1 ^ 2`?

widget.accept: 4: the 1s cancel, the 2s cancel, and 4 is left.
widget.label: Result

hints.text: What is `1 ^ 1`?
Equal values have every bit in common, so XOR clears them all.

feedback.correct: The pairs cancel and the single 4 remains.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. XOR the equal values together first.

byKey.zero: You cancelled the 4 too. It has no partner, so it survives.
byKey.sum: You added them. XOR sets a bit only where exactly one side has it.
byKey.seven: That is `4 | 1 | 2`, an OR. XOR cancels the repeated bits.

explain.text: XOR is order-free, so we may pair equal values: `1 ^ 1 = 0` and `2 ^ 2 = 0`. XOR with 0 changes nothing. So the result is the single value, 4.

screens.title: Three operations
screens.prose: Move `a` and `b` and watch the bits of AND, OR and XOR.

state.caption: AND keeps bits set in both, OR in either, XOR in exactly one

screens.question: Set `a` equal to `b`. Which row always turns into 0?

options.why: With `a` equal to `b`, `a & b` is `a` itself: every bit is set in both.
With `a` equal to `b`, `a | b` is `a` itself.

hints.text: Drag both sliders to the same number.

feedback.correct: `x ^ x` is 0 for every `x`: no bit is set in exactly one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at which row reads 0000 when the two are equal.

explain.text: When `a` equals `b`, every bit is set in both or in neither. XOR keeps bits set in exactly one, so nothing survives. AND and OR both give back `a`.

screens.title: Clearing the lowest bit
screens.prose: Subtracting 1 turns the lowest set bit of `n` off and every bit below it on. So `n & (n - 1)` is `n` with its lowest set bit cleared.
screens.question: Fill in `44 & 43`, and how many times `n &= n - 1` runs before 44 reaches 0.

hints.text: Line up 101100 and 101011.
They agree in the top three bits, 101, and differ below.
`101100 & 101011 = 101000 = 40`. 44 has three set bits, so the loop runs 3 times: 44, 40, 32, 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. AND keeps a bit only where both numbers have it.

byKey.r0c1: Line the two numbers up bit by bit. Only the bits set in both stay.
byKey.r1c1: Each run clears one set bit. Count the 1s in 101100.

explain.text: 44 is 101100 and 43 is 101011; AND keeps 101000, which is 40. Each `n &= n - 1` clears one set bit: 44, 40, 32, 0. So the loop runs once per set bit.

screens.title: Find the single
screens.prose: Every number appears twice except one, which appears once. Numbers may be negative, and the list has odd length. Use $O(1)$ extra memory.
screens.question: Write `single_number(nums)`.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests: one value, negatives, a zero, and 199,999 values in test 7. Each result must equal the expected number.

hints.text: What does XOR do to a pair of equal values?
It cancels them, in any order.
Start with `x = 0` and do `x ^= v` for every value; return `x`.

feedback.correct: One pass, one variable: $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ memory.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 is `[2, 2, 1]`. A sum gives 5; XOR cancels the 2s.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 has negatives. XOR works on Python's negative numbers too.

explain.text: Each pair cancels to 0, and `x ^ 0 = x`, so only the single remains. Python's integers XOR as two's complement, so negatives work. A `Counter` would also pass, with $O(n)$ memory.

screens.title: Isolating the lowest bit
screens.prose: In `contests` l11-bitmasks you met `n & -n`. In two's complement, `-n` flips every bit of `n` and adds 1. Only the lowest set bit of `n` survives the AND.

state.caption: −n flips every bit of n, then adds 1

screens.question: Fill in `12 & -12` and `40 & -40`.

hints.text: They share only the bit worth 4.

feedback.correct: 4 and 8: the lowest set bit of each.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the one bit that `n` and `-n` share.

byKey.r0c1: Compare 00001100 with 11110100. Only one bit is set in both.
byKey.r1c1: Compare 00101000 with 11011000. Only the bit worth 8 is set in both.

explain.text: Flipping makes every bit differ, and adding 1 carries up to the lowest set bit of `n`. That one bit then agrees, and every other bit differs. So `n & -n` isolates it: 4 for 12, 8 for 40.

screens.title: Three of a kind
screens.prose: Now every value appears three times except one: `[2, 2, 2, 7, 7, 7, 5]`. A learner reuses `single_number`.
screens.question: Does XOR still find the single, 5?

options.why: You assumed XOR cancels any repeat. Three equal values leave one copy, so `2 ^ 7 ^ 5` remains, which is 0.

options.text: No: XOR raises an error on repeats
options.why: XOR never raises on integers. It returns a value, just the wrong one.

options.text: Yes, once the list is sorted
options.why: Order never matters to XOR. Three copies still leave one.

hints.text: What is `2 ^ 2 ^ 2`?
Two copies cancel and the third remains: 2.
So the result is `2 ^ 7 ^ 5`. `2 ^ 7` is 5, and `5 ^ 5` is 0.

feedback.correct: Odd repeats survive XOR, so it returns `2 ^ 7 ^ 5 = 0`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out what three copies of one value XOR to.

byKey.b: You assumed XOR cancels any repeat. It cancels pairs only, so each triple leaves one copy behind.

explain.text: XOR cancels in pairs, so three copies leave one. The result is `2 ^ 7 ^ 5`, and 2 is 010, 7 is 111, 5 is 101: they cancel to 0. Counting the ones in each bit column modulo 3 does find 5.

screens.title: Differences over every pair
screens.prose: Return the sum, over every pair of entries (each pair once), of the bit positions where the two differ. Entries run from 0 to 2,147,483,647. Return 0 for fewer than two entries. `contests` l11 counted bits with `p[m] = p[m >> 1] + (m & 1)`; here we count by column.
screens.question: Write `hamming_total(nums)` in $O(32n)$, not over every pair.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests: an empty list, one entry, equal entries, and `range(65536)` in test 8. A double loop over pairs passes the first seven and runs out of time on the eighth.

hints.text: Look at one bit column. Which pairs differ in it?
A pair differs in a column when one entry has a 1 there and the other a 0.
For each of 32 bits count `ones`; that column adds `ones * (len(nums) - ones)`.

feedback.correct: 32 columns, one pass each: linear in $n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 is `[1, 2]`: 01 and 10 differ in both bits, so the answer is 2.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 has 65,536 entries, about 2.1 billion pairs. Count by column instead.

explain.text: In one column, each of `c` entries with a 1 differs from each of `n - c` with a 0. So the column adds `c * (n - c)`, and the columns add up. For `[5, 9, 12]`, three columns add 2 each: 6.

screens.title: The patterns
screens.prose:
What you used, as patterns:

```python
x ^ x == 0; x ^ 0 == x    # pairs cancel
n & (n - 1)               # clear lowest set bit
n & -n                    # isolate lowest set bit
(v >> bit) & 1            # read one bit
n >> 1                    # halve
```
screens.question: Put the steps of `hamming_total` in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: For each of the 32 bit positions, count the entries with a 1 there
Add ones × (n − ones) to the total
Compare every pair of entries bit by bit
lines.why: That is the double loop, about 2 billion pairs at 65,536 entries. The column count does the same work in 32 passes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The count comes before the product.

byKey.d1: You compared pairs. That is correct but quadratic; the columns give the same total in linear time.
byKey.left-out: Every step but one belongs. Only the pairwise comparison is wrong.

explain.text: Each column is independent, so we count its ones once. The product counts the differing pairs in that column. Summing over 32 columns gives the total without listing a single pair.

screens.title: The lost partner
screens.prose: A market data feed sends every message twice, an original and a resend, identified by a sequence number. One resend is lost. The day has 40 million sequence numbers and the checker has little memory.
screens.question: Which way finds the number without a partner in constant extra memory?

options.text: XOR every sequence number: $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ memory
A `Counter` of every number: $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ memory
options.why: It works, but it stores up to 40 million keys. XOR needs one integer.

options.text: Sort the numbers and scan for the unpaired one
options.why: That works in $O(n \log n)$ time and needs the whole day in memory.

options.text: Twice the sum of the distinct numbers, minus the sum of all
options.why: Finding the distinct numbers needs a set: $O(n)$ memory again.

hints.text: Which method keeps only one number in memory?
XOR folds the whole stream into one integer.
Pairs cancel, so the XOR of the stream is the number with no partner: 103 here.

feedback.correct: One pass, one integer: the pairs cancel.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh the memory as well as the time.

byKey.b: You chose a correct method with large memory. XOR gives the same answer in one integer.

explain.text: Every original cancels its resend under XOR, so only the unpartnered number survives. The checker keeps one integer however long the day. In the picture, `101 ^ 102 ^ 101 ^ 103 ^ 102 = 103`.

screens.title: Counting set bits
screens.prose: A mask of positions uses 4 bits, so the masks are the numbers 0 to 15. We want the total number of set bits over all 16 masks.

rows: Set in how many of 0 to 15

screens.question: What is the total number of set bits in 0 to 15?

widget.accept: 32: each of 4 bits is set in 8 of the 16 numbers.
widget.label: Set bits

hints.text: In how many of 0 to 15 is bit 0 set?
Bit 0 is set in every odd number: 8 of 16.
Each of the 4 bits is set in half the numbers: $4 \times 8 = 32$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count by column: each bit is set in half the numbers.

byKey.sixteen: You gave the count of numbers. Count the set bits in all of them.
byKey.max: That is 4 bits times 16 numbers, as if every bit were set. Half of them are.
byKey.fifteen: You counted one bit per number. Most numbers have more than one.

explain.text: Each bit column runs through 0 and 1 equally often over 0 to 15. So each of the 4 columns has 8 ones: 32 in all. Summing `bin(i).count('1')` for 0 to 15 gives the same 32.

ideas: `x ^ x = 0` and `x ^ 0 = x`, in any order, so XOR cancels pairs and finds the single value in $O(1)$ memory.
`n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit and `n & -n` isolates it; `n >> 1` halves.
Count bit by column: a column with `c` ones among `n` entries holds `c * (n - c)` differing pairs.

formula.name: Pairs differing in one bit column

summary.trap: XOR cancels pairs only. With three copies of each value, one copy of each survives and the answer is wrong.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Cancel the equal pairs first.

byKey.zero: 9 has no partner, so it survives.

explain.text: 6, 11 and 13 each appear twice and cancel. XOR with 0 leaves 9.

quiz.question: How many times does `n &= n - 1` run before `n` is 0?

widget.accept: 4: one run per set bit, and 1001101 has four.
widget.label: Runs

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each run clears one set bit.

byKey.seven: That is the number of bits, not the set bits.
byKey.three: Count the 1s in 1001101 again: there are four.

explain.text: `n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit each time. 77 has four set bits, so four runs: 76, 72, 64, then 0.

feedback.correct: The lowest set bit is worth 8.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `n & -n` keeps only the lowest set bit.

byKey.one: Bit 0 of 88 is not set. Find the lowest bit that is.
byKey.sixtyfour: That is the highest set bit.
byKey.cleared: That is `88 & 87`, which clears the lowest bit instead of keeping it.

explain.text: 1011000 ends in three zeros, so its lowest set bit is $2^3 = 8$. `n & -n` keeps exactly that bit.

options.why: XOR cancels pairs. Two of the copies cancel and the third remains.
That is $3 \times 23$, a sum. XOR has no carries.

feedback.correct: Two copies cancel; one is left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Group two of the copies first.

explain.text: `23 ^ 23` is 0, and `0 ^ 23` is 23. Any odd number of copies leaves the value itself.
